stories.t: Final preparations under way for Burlington Art Hop
stories.w: The 34th South End Art Hop opens tonight and runs through Sunday across more than 125 locations along roughly a mile and a half of Pine Street and the roads around it, and artists told NBC5 they have spent months getting ready. SEABA is running shuttles and bike parking, Burlington City Arts has music, visual projects and a kids take and make going all weekend, and Pine Street between Kilburn and

stories.t: Historic dams removed in Smugglers' Notch will reconnect trout habitat
stories.w: Two derelict dams on the Brewster River in Jeffersonville are coming out, the first this week and the second in about two weeks, in a Smugglers' Notch Resort project with the Vermont Natural Resources Council that reconnects roughly 10 miles of trout habitat. The older one, Morse's Mill Dam, is a 50 foot timber crib structure from the late 1800s, and the Burlington connection is direct, since the

stories.t: Is Any Town Willing to Host a 100-Bed Homeless Shelter?
stories.w: CVOEO pulled its proposal for a 100 bed low barrier shelter at the former mattress store at 1717 Williston Road six days before South Burlington's September 8 council meeting, after city staff objected on strained services, crime and transportation grounds. CVOEO and Champlain Housing Trust say they have toured at least a dozen sites across Burlington, Colchester, South Burlington and Shelburne, t

stories.t: The New SEABA Center Is a Hub for Visual and Performing Arts
stories.w: Seven Days' Art Hop guide profiles the SEABA Center, the 7,000 square foot space in the former ArtsRiot building at 400 Pine that the South End Arts + Business Association moved into last fall. stories.t: 'An unprecedented day': How Vermonters learned of 9/11 — and who remembers 25 years later
stories.w: Today is the 25th anniversary, and Kevin O'Connor's first person column for VTDigger tells it from the Vermont side, through Rutland native Michael Rosen watching from a block and a half away, former Port Authority officer Norma Hardy, who later became Vermont's first Black female police chief, and Bishop Kenneth Angell, whose brother David died on the first plane. stories.t: Expecting Trouble: Vermonters Are Losing Local Birth Centers
stories.w: Seven Days' long feature on maternity care traces how Springfield closed its labor and delivery unit in 2019, Copley closed in 2025, and nearly one in three Vermonters giving birth now lives outside the recommended 30 minute drive to hospital obstetric care. UVM Health's three Vermont hospitals with labor and delivery lost a combined $4 million on it last year, with UVM Medical Center itself rough

stories.t: In reversal, Brattleboro Memorial Hospital will keep its birth center open
stories.w: Brattleboro Memorial announced Thursday evening it will keep its birth center open after all, reversing a July decision to close it on December 31. The hospital credits funding approved September 8 through the state's federally funded Rural Health Transformation Program, $325,000 in pledged community donations, and an efficiency plan worked out with its obstetrics staff, and it says the final gran

stories.t: Vermont regulators finalize 5.5% rate increase for Green Mountain Power customers
stories.w: The Public Utility Commission approved a 5.5% increase for Green Mountain Power's more than 275,000 Vermont customers, down from the 7.5% the utility asked for, and it takes effect October 1. Regulators approved about $113 million of the $341 million in four year resilience spending GMP requested, and the utility says storms are the reason it needs the money. stories.t: Vermont Creemee Supply Disrupted by Immigration Enforcement
stories.w: Kingdom Creamery of Vermont, the largest supplier of Vermont made creemee mix, cut production to a limited basis after Border Patrol detained three of its migrant workers in late July, all three were deported, and more employees left out of fear. Stands from Bristol to Montpelier have been scrambling for substitute mix from Miller Farm in Vernon or HP Hood in Massachusetts, and Holy Halvah in Bris

stories.t: Vermont awards first batch of $195 million in federal rural health funds
stories.w: Vermont announced the first $11.7 million of its $195 million in federal Rural Health Transformation money, with $9 million going to the Vermont Student Assistance Corporation for tuition benefits for healthcare students who commit to five years working in state and $2.7 million to three nursing homes and four teaching institutions for licensed nursing assistant training. The state has to allocate

stories.t: Federal judge blocks Vermont AG's probe of 'Planet Hank' AI video
stories.w: Senior U.S. District Judge William K. Sessions III issued a preliminary injunction barring Attorney General Charity Clark's office from enforcing a civil investigative demand against Hank Poitras over an AI generated satirical video of Rep. Becca Balint and candidate Mark Coester, the first real court test of Act 75, Vermont's new law on deceptive AI election media. The judge found the video ridic

stories.t: Ray's Is Closing Its Essex Junction Market. It's Also the Hub of a Fish Trade Almost No Other State Allows
stories.w: We ran the closing news last month, and the last day is now here. Ray's Seafood Market & Restaurant closes its Pine Crest Drive location in Essex Junction for good on Saturday at 7 PM after 74 years, so this weekend is the last chance for a lap. Compass Vermont's piece from August explains the part most customers never knew, which is that Ray's second site on North Street in Burlington is the hub

stories.t: Album Review: Lily Seabird, 'Lightspheres on Their Way'
stories.w: Seven Days reviews Burlington songwriter Lily Seabird's new album Lightspheres on Their Way, out last week on Lame-O Records, and hears a turn toward louder, Crazy Horse style distortion after 2021's Beside Myself and last year's Trash Mountain. The record is only partly on streaming, so the reviewer's advice is to buy a copy at a local record store, and she plays Foam Brewers on November 15.

Burlington Technical Center opens permanent home at new high school
stories.w: Six years after PCB concerns closed the old building, the Burlington Technical Center's five programs are finally back under one roof at the new Burlington High School, with additional offerings at the airport. Students walked into classrooms ranging from a criminal justice suite with an interrogation room to a health science academy built around a real-world hospital environment. Director Jason R

stories.t: Ribbon cutting celebrates completion of Burlington Wildways Trail
stories.w: Nearly ten years in the making, the ten mile Wildways Trail is officially complete, linking the Intervale, Ethan Allen Homestead, Ethan Allen Park and Rock Point in one continuous route from the Winooski River to Lake Champlain. Saturday's ribbon cutting at the Homestead ended the only way it should have, with a guided hike, and the full route is now open to everyone.

stories.t: Burlington mayor meets with businesses over downtown disorder
stories.w: A standing room only crowd packed City Hall on Friday as downtown businesses told Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak they are losing patience with open drug use, vagrancy and safety issues, with the Friendly Toast's manager describing a recent needle stick and Vermont Pub and Brewery reporting foot traffic down 20 percent from an already bad year. stories.t: Why Vermont's housing shortage can't be explained by population size alone
stories.w: If the population is flat, why is it still so hard to find a place to live? This deep dive lands on household size, with 70 percent of Vermont households now just one or two people and the state average down to 2.2, one of the smallest in the country. The same number of people simply takes up more homes, and the Vermont Housing Finance Agency calculates the state needed nearly 22,000 additional ho

stories.t: Gov. Scott calls proposed 100-bed shelter in Chittenden County a bad idea
stories.w: The governor doubled down on his criticism of the City Council's 10-point homelessness resolution, saying he was surprised to see the 100-bed low barrier shelter on the list and that he would rather see smaller shelters spread across the county. He also suggested Vermonters elsewhere might be miffed at Burlington asking for extra resources when other regions face the same problems. Paired with Fri

stories.t: UVM president says school's budget deficit is closed despite declining enrollment
stories.w: President Marlene Tromp used her first State of the University address to announce the projected $12 million deficit is fully closed, done through eliminating vacant positions and operational inefficiencies rather than layoffs. Enrollment is still the headwind, with about 2,600 first years against a usual target of 3,000 and roughly 10,800 students overall as the demographic cliff hits New England

stories.t: 49,000 Vermonters could lose Medicaid in the new year
stories.w: Federal Medicaid changes hit in waves, with several hundred immigrants losing eligibility October 1 and up to 49,000 Vermonters at risk on January 1 when new work requirements take effect, requiring at least $580 in monthly income or 80 hours of work, school, training or community service. Reviews also go to every six months starting in 2027. The state has launched StayCoveredVT.com so people can

stories.t: Abuse claimants fight Vermont Catholic Church plan to sell Rice Memorial High to supporters
stories.w: Lawyers for more than 100 clergy abuse claimants are challenging the diocese's plan to sell Rice Memorial High School to a supporter group for $4.3 million, just 14 percent of the $30.5 million value in the church's own appraisal, noting the property was never listed, brokered or opened to competing offers. The creditors want a public sale to raise more money for abuse settlements, while the dioce

stories.t: The Closures of Four Dairy Plants Lead to Worry in Vermont
stories.w: Four milk processing plants have closed or announced closures in a matter of months, in Barre, Georgia, Enosburg Falls and St. Albans, and the losses have farmers and state leaders worried about the $5.4 billion dairy sector's future. stories.t: 'I'll take money from anyone': Corporate cash fuels some Vermont political campaigns
stories.w: A Vermont Public analysis found Gov. Scott has taken $167,700 from corporations, businesses and corporate PACs over three cycles, 22.7 percent of his donations, while Attorney General Charity Clark has accepted $84,000, including checks from gambling companies and firms her office regulates or has sued. stories.t: Problem Properties: Burlington publishes list of noncompliant vacant buildings
stories.w: The city published a top ten list of noncompliant vacant buildings, naming properties like the old Bove's on Pearl Street, vacant since 2019 with violations that make it unsafe for emergency crews to enter, and a former gas station with no redevelopment plans. Owners on the list owe fees under the vacant building ordinance or have visible maintenance problems, and one landlord with two listed prop

stories.t: As Trump tries to curtail mail-in voting, Vermont officials clean up errors on state voter rolls
stories.w: The state removed just under 900 people from the voter rolls who were wrongly registered by DMV clerical errors going back 25 years, none of whom ever cast a ballot, all of whom had actively declined registration. Gov. Scott and Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas announced the cleanup themselves, framing it as getting the rolls airtight before general election ballots mail out next month, on

stories.t: New rules for Vermont vehicle inspections begin next month
stories.w: Starting September 1, your car can no longer fail inspection for rotor rust, tire cuts, windshield cracks or ABS and airbag warning lights, though mechanics can still recommend the fixes. If a station fails you solely for one of those, the DMV Highway Patrol says report it and they will investigate.

stories.t: Apps entice young Vermonters to join the 'birding boom'
stories.w: Free apps like Merlin Bird ID and eBird are pulling Gen Z into a hobby long associated with the 55 and up crowd, and the local numbers back it up, with UVM's ornithology class doubling to around 60 students a semester and campus Audubon chapters nationally growing from a dozen to over 92 since 2019. Young Burlington birders describe group chats that light up when a good bird shows at Colchester Po

Burlington Named the #3 Best US City to Work
stories.w: An Indeed study of metro areas over 200,000 ranked Burlington third in the country for work, behind only Boston and Washington DC and ahead of San Jose and San Francisco. The ranking weighed six pillars, from compensation to work-life balance, and our win came on job opportunity, where apparently Burlington posted the highest score in the nation. stories.t: ‘Watershed moment’: Vermont secures $92.7M and new restrictions for teens in Meta settlement
stories.w: Attorney General Charity Clark's 2023 lawsuit against Meta ended this week in the largest single-company settlement in state history, $92.7 million plus a decade of required protections for users under 18, including a nighttime block, a 2 hour daily limit, better age verification and a school mode that quiets notifications during the day. stories.t: Burlington Police arrest 11 people during month of drug operations in City Hall Park
stories.w: Burlington Police worked with the DEA and ATF on a multi-week covert operation in City Hall Park that produced 11 drug-related arrests between August 6 and 26, with plainclothes officers watching the park and its edges all month. stories.t: Burlington Asks Again for State Help With Public Safety Problems
stories.w: In a rare moment of consensus, the City Council passed a unanimous resolution alongside Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak asking Gov. Phil Scott for immediate help on homelessness and public safety. stories.t: Burlington artist dug Nap pleads not guilty in death of teen cyclist
stories.w: Douglas Knapp, 79, the folk artist known around town as dug Nap, pleaded not guilty Thursday to negligent operation with death resulting in the July crash that killed 16 year old Shiloh Skalka, a rising junior at Burlington High School riding her e-bike. The newly public affidavit says Skalka activated the flashing crosswalk signal at Pine and Locust, waited about 3 seconds, and was struck by Knap

stories.t: New students arrive at UVM as city, campus step up safety measures
stories.w: UVM move-in is underway, and both the university and the city are leaning into safety this year, with required safety modules before arrival, the CatSafe app connecting students to campus police or BPD around the clock, and a resource list from the mayor's office that includes a drug trafficking tipline. stories.t: Halfway through Vermont's first ever Navy Week
stories.w: Burlington Navy Week rolls on through Sunday, with ship demonstrations, live drills and daily Navy band music on the waterfront, plus a Navy presence at the fair starting today. stories.t: Rough pavement on I-89 caused by "raveling," VTrans says
stories.w: If you've felt your car wander in the right lane of I-89 between Montpelier and St. Albans, there's now a name for it. VTrans chief engineer Jeremy Reed says those grooves come from raveling rather than rutting, the top layer of pavement disintegrating so that in the worst spots you're driving on the layer underneath. stories.t: 15 years after Irene, plucky business owners recall the monster storm and its aftermath
stories.w: Fifteen years ago today, Tropical Storm Irene sent rivers over their banks across Vermont, and this remembrance from Wilmington captures what that Sunday cost. Bartleby's Books took 3.5 feet of water and lost 85% of its inventory, roughly $400,000 in damage with less than half insured, and the flood line on Town Hall still sits a few inches above the 1938 record. stories.t: Vermont's bear population is booming. So is conflict with humans
stories.w: Vermont's game wardens have fielded roughly 1,800 bear calls so far this year, on pace for a record, and one bear in Jamaica ransacked a house and left the stove burner on. stories.t: Vital Communities enters talks to save town listservs from shutdown
stories.w: The 38 town listservs of the Upper Valley got a stay of execution. After Vital Communities announced it would stop supporting the two decade old email lists, community backlash bought a delay, and a group of residents and list managers is now forming a nonprofit called UV Lists to take them over this fall, with subscribers promised the same emails from a new domain for about $10,000 a year in tech

stories.t: Veterans Affairs to open clinic in South Burlington
stories.w: The VA signed a 20 year lease for a new outpatient clinic at Technology Park in South Burlington, expected to open by 2030 and replace the current Burlington clinic. The new spot puts roughly 7,900 veterans within an hour's drive, and the 24,000 square foot space adds mental health services plus physical and occupational therapy to the primary care, optometry and audiology already offered. Burlington prepares to host first-ever Navy Week
stories.w: Burlington Navy Week runs Monday through Sunday, the first Navy Week ever held in Vermont, and most of it is free and on the waterfront. A 34 foot Sea Ark harbor patrol boat does demonstrations off the Community Boathouse Monday and next Friday at 11:30, sailors from the namesake USS Montpelier and USNS Burlington are on display between ECHO and the Boathouse from noon to 5:30 Monday through Thurs

stories.t: Vermont's Miss Black USA reflects on historic win
stories.w: Harmony Edosomwan, who owns Harmony's Kitchen in Winooski and cooks traditional Black Southern food there, took home the national crown at this year's Miss Black USA pageant. Along with the title she won a full ride to law school, and she says she wants to use the platform to bring more attention to people of color living in Vermont.

stories.t: Vermont State Police patrols end in Burlington following violent weekend
stories.w: The state police pulled their extra downtown patrols Sunday after three weeks, an assignment Gov. Phil Scott ordered ahead of the New England governors and Eastern Canadian premiers conference. The weekend they left brought a stabbing near Bank and St. Paul, the fatal stabbing behind Courthouse Plaza, an exchange of gunfire on lower Church Street and a separate accidental discharge. stories.t: Suspect surrenders and faces second-degree murder charge in downtown Burlington stabbing
stories.w: Hassan O. Haji, 24, of Winooski, walked into Burlington police headquarters Tuesday morning and pleaded not guilty that afternoon to second degree murder in the Saturday stabbing behind the Main Street courthouse we noted Monday. stories.t: The Skinny Pancake Partners with Vermont Brewers in BTV and Quechee
stories.w: Starting today, the bar at the waterfront Skinny Pancake on Lake Street becomes a Lawson's Finest tap takeover that runs through foliage season, every tap pouring the Waitsfield brewery's beer, including the Sip line, with the new nonalcoholic Sip'N IPA in cans. Burlington High School opens new building in two weeks. Here's what's inside.
stories.w: Five years after PCBs pushed BHS students into the old downtown Macy's, the new building is ready, with a gym, an auditorium, soundproof music rooms, and an accessible balcony added from public feedback. It holds 1,100 students, comfortably ahead of the 960 currently enrolled across the high school and tech center. The ribbon-cutting is this Saturday, August 22, and the district is running free pu

stories.t: How Amanda Janoo, a progressive political outsider, won Vermont's Democratic primary for governor
stories.w: Janoo, an economist who had never run for office, took last week's primary 49.1 to 46.5 in unofficial results despite trailing Aly Richards in money and endorsements, and now faces Gov. Phil Scott in November. Analysts credit her plain talk on economic inequality and her read as the authentic change candidate, while a pro-Richards PAC's ad blitz, funded mostly from out of state, may have backfired

stories.t: Sneakers Bistro Goes Nighttime With Sneakeasy Cocktail Lounge
stories.w: Bar manager Yassen Zech and lead bartender Rachel Mutino designed the menu and the thrifted decor lounge together, with drinks like a clarified Bloody Mary martini and bar bites that nod to Belizean fry jacks. A series of soft openings leads up to the launch, and daytime service stays exactly as it was.

stories.t: Champlain Valley Fair comes to life with live artist demonstrations
stories.w: The fair's art exhibition (August 28 through September 6) is getting a gallery style refresh this year, with featured linocut printmaker Lauren McCabe and the Essex Art League carving and painting live for fairgoers. Around 500 public submissions get juried into categories that this year include Haunted and Just Desserts. If you want in, free online entry closes this Thursday, August 20, with drop

stories.t: Lake Champlain Chamber launches "Downtown Business Alliance"
stories.w: The Chamber's new advocacy division is meant to give downtown businesses a dedicated voice with city and state leaders as the core wrestles with public safety and economic uncertainty. It wants an advisory board seated by October 1 and is hiring a Downtown Advocacy Manager to track ordinances and represent businesses before the city council. stories.t: Three Teens Run the Show at Essex Junction's Black Ice Premium Ice Cream
stories.w: The scoop shop at 34 Park Street in Essex Junction is run by three brothers, 13-year-old twins Malachi and Messiah and 14-year-old Jaleel, who co-own it with their dad. They handle the scooping, the marketing, and the operations themselves, with ice cream from Woodstock's Mountain Creamery. Open daily 3 to 9 through October.

stories.t: South Burlington considers eminent domain for Long Property easement
stories.w: The city council is starting eminent domain proceedings for a road right-of-way on the 36-acre Long Property on Spear Street, where a 12-townhome Habitat for Humanity project is planned. The review board had to deny the application in July because the landowner would not include an easement for a future road the official city map requires, which started a 120-day clock for the city to act. stories.t: Fluency gives infrastructure they need to trust AI
stories.w: The Burlington ad-tech company says its platform now drives $3 billion in annual ad spend across a quarter million monthly campaigns, with AI generating the creative while a deterministic layer keeps actual budgets inside advertiser guardrails. stories.t: Montréal Critic Lesley Chesterman Shares Her Restaurant Intel
stories.w: Seven Days sat down with the Gazette's longtime restaurant critic, then built a 30-hour Montréal eating itinerary from her tips, from pastries at Rhubarbe to rotisserie chicken at La Lune to dinner at Le Violon. stories.t: Plans to demolish old Bove's restaurant in Burlington put on hold
stories.w: The Bove family has pulled its permits to replace the old Pearl Street restaurant with a six-story, 25-unit housing building, citing interest rates, construction costs, and the wave of other housing projects underway in Chittenden County. The building has sat vacant since 2015 and ranks among the city's ten most non-compliant properties, but a city ordinance bars tearing down historic buildings wi

stories.t: A day in the life of a UVM Extension Master Gardener
stories.w: The Observer profiles Sue Stanne, a 23-year veteran of the program and one of 442 Master Gardener volunteers statewide, who spends Thursdays fielding plant mysteries on the Extension Helpline. Her projects run from the Vermont Respite House gardens to a donation plot at the Williston Community Garden to a new community gardening shed at The Farm at South Village. stories.t: 'Valley Transit' Films in the Upper Valley
stories.w: Believed to be the first feature film shot entirely in the Upper Valley, Valley Transit is filming with an all-local cast and crew as the centerpiece of a summer intensive that pairs students with professionals.
